source.title: An Effective Label Noise Model for DNN Text Classification
source.authors: Ishan Jindal; Daniel Pressel; Brian Lester; Matthew S. Nokleby

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no obvious truncation or corruption materially prevents extraction, although Table 2 is flattened and its cell-to-column mapping is partly ambiguous.
record.tranche_reason: Tests label-noise behavior in text CNNs with a noise-model layer and a standard-network baseline. Its baseline results refine the random-label fitting claim: on several text datasets, standard networks’ test accuracy degrades toward chance under high random label noise, but the paper does not report training error or a completely random labeling of the entire training set.
record.gate_note: Results concern artificially corrupted text-classification labels and test accuracy. Table 2 reports separate dataset, noise type, corruption level, and model results, but flattened layout makes many cell mappings unclear; only unambiguous text-described results are extracted. The claim versions concern image labels, completely random labels, and other specified behaviors, which this study generally does not test.
record.test_reason: The standard text-CNN baselines test V4's prediction that clean-test performance deteriorates as uniform label corruption increases. They do not establish perfect training fit. Text inputs are within the stated versions' scope; the versions are not restricted to images.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that a properly initialized and regularized nonlinear noise layer absorbs label noise and improves sentence representations. They interpret the baseline representations as fitting noisy labels, but do not report training error establishing perfect memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Text classification with injected class-conditional or instance-dependent label noise; adds a learned nonlinear noise-model layer and reports test accuracy, rather than testing image classification under completely random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise-model initialization and regularization affect performance; the authors report that the identity initialization with gain equal to the number of classes works best in their DBpedia experiment. Batch size gives small gains for highly non-uniform noise, but no gains for uniform flips.

fits_no_version.finding: The added noise layer improves clean-test classification and representation quality; its initialization and regularization affect performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A suitably initialized and regularized noise layer improves text classification under corrupted supervision.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard-CNN representations qualitatively cluster according to supplied noisy labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text CNN representations can encode partially corrupted training labels.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper reports mean accuracy over five runs but no error bars. Table 2 is flattened in the supplied text, making many precise row-to-cell assignments uncertain. The experiments use text data and partial label corruption, so they do not directly establish the image-based claim versions. No training-error measure is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 contains many dataset, model, noise-type, and corruption-level combinations, but the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve all cell mappings. To avoid assigning ambiguous values to models or conditions, most such entries are omitted; see Table 2. Figure 2 and Figure 3 results are figure-only and are not extracted as numeric rows.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error under completely random labels, chance test performance under that condition, and unchanged training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout the corruption range, memorization of corrupted examples, and the endpoint at completely random labels. Uniform corruption is not evaluated through p=1.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms clean-label generalization. Regularizing the added noise layer addresses a different question.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels; the visualizations do not establish this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly restricts the claims to images and understates the experimental corruption range: Table 2 includes DBpedia noise levels through 90%. Under Equation 1, p is the uniform-redraw mixture weight; actual label disagreement is p(1−1/K). All experiments use early stopping on corrupted validation labels. Additional Table 2 combinations and figure results are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies label corruption in text datasets only up to 70% in its general setting; it does not test a completely random labeling or report training error.
Does not report training time or convergence speed by corruption fraction.
Does not test shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Reports test accuracy under partial label noise, but does not report perfect training fit across noise levels or test error through 100% random corruption.
Does not test whether regularization, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms generalization on true labels.
Does not measure whether real patterns are learned before noisy labels during training; t-SNE visualizations concern a noise-model system, not the stated learning-order claim.
